why: The api mints these on Node and a Cloudflare Worker validates them on workerd. Every
assertion that signs and verifies with one implementation passes on self-consistent
nonsense: mutating the signed separator or the expiry compare left the whole media suite
green. These are literal expected values, so an implementation that changes stops matching.
Generated by a path that shares no code with the module under test:
printf '%s' "$KEY:$EXP" | openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET" -binary \
| openssl base64 -A | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '='
IMMUTABLE. A change to the signing scheme is a NEW vector set with a new version, never an
edit to this one, for the same reason an applied migration is never edited.
APPENDED 2026-08-21: the `rotation` and `parity` sections at the foot of this file. Both
are appends and not edits, and the paragraph above is exactly what draws the line. Neither
changes the SCHEME. Rotation is the same HMAC-SHA256 over the same `${objectKey}:${exp}`
message with a different key; parity is the same HMAC over a constant. Nothing above them
moved, no existing value was recomputed, and the version stays 1 because a verifier reading
version 1 still reads the same scheme it always did. A change to the scheme itself would
still be a new file at version 2 rather than anything in here.
Every appended value came from the same openssl pipeline recorded above, run over the
message its own section names. None of it came from the module the tests point at, which
is the entire reason this file exists.
APPENDED 2026-08-21, later the same day: the `routing` section. Also an append and not an
edit, and it touches the signature not at all: bucket routing reads the first path segment
of an object key and never hashes anything. So there is no openssl command behind these
values and there should not be one. They are expectations about which bucket a key may be
read from, and the correct expectation for almost all of them is `null`, meaning refuse
before touching R2. They were written from the rule stated in `bucketRoleForObjectKey`,
not from what the function returned, which matters because the function disagreed with its
own documented rule when they were written.

why: Key rotation, from the verifier's side. `verifyMediaSignature` takes either one secret or
an ORDERED list, current key first, and accepts when any of them matches.
`secrets` below is the literal argument, in order. `signedWith` names which key minted
`sig`, so the server-side test can re-derive it with node:crypto without interpreting
anything. The three secrets are `secret` above, `previousSecret` and `strangerSecret`
here. All three are vectors-only strings that have never signed anything real.
The rotation these describe: set the Worker's previous key to the old secret and its
current key to the new one, then flip the api's single key. URLs minted in the hour before
the flip keep resolving until they expire. The api never verifies, so it never holds two.

the ordinary case during a rotation: minted by the current key, both offered
order independence: the previous key's URL against a reversed list
order independence: the current key's URL against a reversed list
a one-element list is the plain string, and accepts what the string accepts
an EMPTY list refuses a perfectly good signature: a keyless rotation fails closed
a key neither side holds, refused with both real keys offered
still valid at the exact millisecond of expiry, list or no list
expired one millisecond later, so no key in the list can rescue it

why: The parity canary. Both the api and the Worker sign one constant with their own copy of
MEDIA_SIGNING_SECRET and publish the first 8 characters, so `curl` against each side and
one `diff` answers 'do these two hold the same secret'. A mismatch presents as every photo
403ing, which looks exactly like a broken Worker rather than a wrong password.
`message` is PARITY_MESSAGE, asserted equal to the exported constant so the two cannot
drift. `signature` is the full 43 characters and `fingerprint` is the published prefix,
recorded separately so that taking the wrong number of characters cannot pass.
Generated with the same openssl pipeline as everything above, over the constant:
printf '%s' 'clubchat-media-signing-parity-v1' \
| openssl dgst -sha256 -hmac "$SECRET" -binary \
| openssl base64 -A | tr '+/' '-_' | tr -d '=' | cut -c1-8

the previous vectors secret, which is what a Worker mid-rotation reports

why: Which bucket a key may be read from, decided by its FIRST PATH SEGMENT and nothing else.
No HMAC is involved, so unlike every other section here these values came from the rule
rather than from openssl. The rule, stated in full so a reader never has to infer it:
a key routes only when it has a slash, the text before that slash is non-empty, and
that text is exactly one of the kinds in MEDIA_KINDS. Anything else is null.
Null is a refusal and the edge answers 404 on it WITHOUT reading a bucket. That is the
security property the whole section exists to hold: routing an unrecognised prefix to the
private bucket would turn a typo into a probe of private content.
Why this table is shaped the way it is. On 2026-08-21 a red-team pass found that
`bucketRoleForObjectKey` computed its prefix as `slice(0, indexOf('/'))`, and indexOf
answers -1 when there is no slash, which slice reads as `drop the last character` rather
than as `nothing`. So a SLASHLESS key whose final character removal lands on a real kind
routed to a real bucket: `photos` was read as `photo`, `avatars` as `avatar`, `documents`
as `document`. Driven end to end in workerd it returned 200 with bytes out of the private
bucket. The existing tests missed exactly this shape, and it is worth understanding why:
they covered `photos/2026-04/x`, which HAS a slash and so has a genuinely unknown prefix,
and `photo`, which loses a real character and becomes `phot`. Neither is the broken case.
The table below therefore pairs each slashless near-miss with the slashed spelling of the
same string, because only the pair distinguishes the two.
It was never reachable from the internet: the api signs only `${kind}/${YYYY-MM}/${uuid}`,
so no signature for a slashless key can be obtained. It is recorded here anyway because a
documented security property that is false is worse than one that was never claimed.
